talks.title: Hoedown Roundup: Wrangling Active Directory Misconfigurations, Texas Style!
talks.teaser: Presents hoedown Roundup: Wrangling Active Directory Misconfigurations, Texas Style and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: A Security Fest presenter delivers "Hoedown Roundup," a Texas-themed guide to wrangling Active Directory misconfigurations from a purple team perspective.

Key Topics: Active Directory fundamentals and domain controller roles; common AD misconfigurations exploited in assessments; purple team methodology combining offensive findings with defensive validation; and security operations as unsung heroes.

Technical Details: The speaker explains domain controllers as authentication authorities processing access requests based on directory permissions, then walks through typical assessment approaches for identifying exploitable AD misconfigurations in enterprise environments.

Takeaways: AD misconfigurations remain a primary attack path in enterprise environments. Purple teams should systematically assess and remediate directory permissions, delegation, and authentication weaknesses.

talks.title: Guardians of the Hypervisor: ESXi Ransomware Incident Response
talks.teaser: Details guardians of the Hypervisor: ESXi Ransomware Incident Response and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
ESXi Ransomware Reality Check

Truesec incident responders Anders and Nicholas open by showing ESXi “exec install only” whitelisting can stop foreign code—but attackers with root can disable it with a one-liner. They share experience from roughly 100 ESXi ransomware cases.

vSphere Architecture and Risk

vCenter Server runs on VMware Photon Linux; ESXi hosts run VMs but are not full Linux, lack onboard EDR, emit heavy syslog, and rebuild filesystems each boot—complicating persistence yet enabling binary whitelisting when properly locked down. Ransomware groups adapted Linux encryptors around 2021 to encrypt entire hypervisor estates in one sweep.

Typical Attack Path and Defense

Most incidents (~80–90%) follow AD foothold to vCenter via AD-authenticated admin login rather than exotic exploits. Victims often lacked architecture hardening and managed detection on surrounding infrastructure. The talk covers real attack mechanics, recovery, and layered protection so organizations avoid the “worst day at work” scenario.

talks.title: UnRegister Me: hunting and securing user registration vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Outlines unRegister Me: hunting and securing user registration vulnerabilities and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Why Registration Bugs Matter

A Microsoft senior red teamer shares field notes on authentication and authorization flaws rooted in user registration across web and mobile apps. Because registration is the weakest entry point, these bugs often yield account takeover without traditional privilege escalation.

OTP and Identity Assumptions

The talk dissects phone-number OTP flows where email is collected but never verified. Attackers register high-value emails like executive addresses using their own phone, exploiting users' tendency to trust email identities over phone numbers in chat and collaboration apps.

Chaining Low-Severity Issues

A case study shows registration returning a long-lived pin, an active post-registration endpoint, and an API that leaks authentication tokens. Chained together, an attacker maintains persistent access even after the victim resets credentials via forgot-password.

Pre-Registration Account Takeover

The speaker introduces pre-registration ATO: controlling an account slot before the legitimate user arrives. Manual hunting produces little noise and evades typical detection because activity resembles legitimate user behavior. Fixes require email verification, disabling registration endpoints after signup, and never returning sensitive tokens.

talks.title: How not to implement secure digital identity: Poland's Digital ID system
talks.teaser: Discusses how not to implement secure digital identity: Polands Digital ID system and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Szymon, an IT security consultant at SecuRing specializing in mobile application security, presents research evaluating the security architecture of Poland's national digital identity system, mObywatel (M-Citizen). The talk analyzes the system's compliance with the EU eIDAS regulation and the Polish M-Citizen Application Act, which legally mandates broad commercial and governmental acceptance. Szymon demonstrates severe vulnerabilities across the system's visual, functional, and cryptographic verification mechanisms, revealing how attackers can bypass physical checks, conduct targeted QR phishing, and impersonate victims at high-security institutions like banks.

Key Topics:
- Regulatory foundation under EU eIDAS and the Polish M-Citizen Application Act
- Three-tiered verification model: visual, functional, and cryptographic verification
- Client-side data manipulation via the proof-of-concept "mHacker" injection tool
- Flaws in cryptographic verification: unauthenticated QR metadata phishing and container signature logic bypass

Technical Details:
The mObywatel system features three verification tiers: visual verification (inspecting holographic animations, gyroscope responses, and timestamps), functional verification (instructing the user to interact with the app, such as re-logging or switching modules), and cryptographic verification (a mutual QR-code-mediated protocol exchanging data via government servers). In real-world assessments across high-risk entities—including medical clinics, airports, and telecommunications stores—Szymon discovered that staff universally relied only on visual verification. Exploiting this operational deficiency, he developed "mHacker," a proof-of-concept utility that modifies the legitimate application's memory on the fly. This permitted instantaneous alteration of photos, names, and national identification numbers (PESEL) without restarting the application, successfully allowing unauthorized SIM-card swaps at telecom providers and physical access bypasses during penetration tests. Only banking institutions enforced the highest tier of cryptographic verification.

Investigating the technical protocol, onboarding involves a trusted third party (such as a bank) transmitting user data out-of-band to government servers, which returns an encrypted "government-signed container" (a signed JSON blob holding personal attributes) and a user personal certificate stored in the mobile device's Secure Element. During cryptographic verification, the verifier displays a QR code containing transaction metadata. Szymon revealed that the QR code's "Creator name" field lacked cryptographic integrity; an attacker could inject newline characters to push disclosure warnings off-screen, creating a deceptive fishing interface that harvests a victim's personal data. Crucially, Szymon uncovered a fatal server-side business logic vulnerability: during mutual verification, the government server failed to validate whether the submitted digital container belonged to the identity on the signing personal certificate. By phishing a victim's government-signed container and signing it with the attacker's own valid personal certificate, an attacker could present the victim's identity to a verifier (like a bank), achieving fully valid cryptographic verification on both iOS and Android.

Key Takeaways:
Digital identity architectures cannot rely on visual or functional inspection on mobile screens, as client-side memory manipulation trivializes graphical authenticity checks. Verifiers handling sensitive transactions must mandate end-to-end cryptographic verification. Furthermore, central government authentication backends must enforce strict cryptographic binding between the identity claimed within data containers and the public key certificate used to sign verification requests.
